in_context.text: The elder has just praised Gaius for helping travelling Christian workers who went out for Christ's name and took nothing from the Gentiles. This verse draws the conclusion: believers ought to welcome such workers, and by doing so they share in the work of the truth. It sets up the contrast with Diotrephes, who refused to receive them.

speaker.text: "The elder," who does not give his name. Early Christian tradition identifies him as John the apostle. Some scholars think he was a different church leader.

audience.text: Gaius, a believer the elder loves and counts among his children in the faith. The "we" includes the elder, Gaius and believers like them.

affected.text: The travelling brethren and strangers who went out for Christ's name and depended on churches to house them and send them on.

what.text: The verse states a duty: we ought to receive and welcome such workers. It gives the reason: so that we become fellow workers with the truth they carry. Paul uses similar language of believers as labourers together with God.

events.text: The letter describes an ongoing situation. Workers had come to Gaius's church, and Gaius had helped them. Diotrephes was turning such visitors away.

written.text: Traditional view: about AD 85-95, around the time of 1 and 2 John. Scholarly view: most scholars also place it in the late first century, while some think the elder was not the apostle.

where.text: The letter does not say where it was written. Early tradition places John's last years in Ephesus. It was sent to a church where Gaius lived, likely in the province of Asia.

purpose.text: To commend Gaius's hospitality and urge it as a shared duty. It also prepares for the elder's rebuke of Diotrephes, who would not receive the brethren.

big_picture.text: Those who support gospel workers share in the work itself. The New Testament elsewhere speaks of believers as labourers together with God and fellowlabourers in the gospel.

for_readers.text: Not everyone travels or preaches. But welcoming and helping those who do is a real way to take part in spreading the truth.

why_it_matters.text: The word means to owe or be a debtor. With a following verb it means to be bound or obliged to do something, as in John 13:14. Welcoming these workers is a duty, not merely a kindness.
Here the word means to receive, welcome or entertain. The lexicon lists this verse for that sense. It points to practical hospitality like the help Gaius gave.

The word means a fellow worker. Paul uses it of his co-workers, as in Romans 16:3 and Philippians 2:25, and of believers as God's fellow workers in 1 Corinthians 3:9. Here it places those who give hospitality alongside the workers themselves.
The word can mean religious truth, especially Christian teaching, or sincerity of character. Truth runs through this letter: Gaius walks in the truth (1:3-4).

takeaway.text: Welcoming and supporting those who serve Christ is something believers owe. By doing it, they become partners in the work of the truth.

resolved.reason: It cites 1:7 (workers going out for Christ's name) as an example of the truth theme, but that verse does not mention truth. The verses that actually show the theme are 1:3-4.
